cards.subject: A discovery call
says: is the first structured conversation held to learn the buyer's situation before anything is proposed
spends most of its time on the buyer's problems rather than on the seller's service
cards.use: need to find out what a prospect is actually trying to fix
not: is a full product demonstration delivered from the first minute

cards.subject: An open question
says: begins with words such as what, how or tell me about
invites a full answer in the buyer's own words
cards.use: want the buyer to explain their situation rather than just confirm it
not: can be fully answered with a single word

cards.subject: A closed question
says: can be answered with yes, no or a single fact
confirms a detail once the wider picture is already clear
cards.use: need to confirm a specific date, number or name
not: draws out the buyer's full story better than any other form

cards.subject: A pain point
says: is a specific problem that costs the buyer time, money or risk
gives the buyer a reason to act now rather than later
cards.use: hear a buyer describe something that keeps going wrong
not: is a feature the seller wants to highlight

cards.subject: A desired outcome
says: describes the result the buyer wants to see once the work is done
is best stated by the buyer in measurable terms
cards.use: need to know what success looks like for this buyer
not: is a list of the seller's deliverables

cards.subject: An impact question
says: asks what a problem costs the buyer if it carries on
turns a vague annoyance into a case with a figure attached
cards.use: need to size the cost of a problem the buyer has only mentioned in passing
not: asks the buyer to rank the seller's features

cards.subject: Summarising back
says: repeats the buyer's situation in the seller's own words to confirm it
shows the buyer they were understood before any solution is offered
cards.use: want to check you have understood a long explanation correctly
not: moves straight to quoting a price

cards.subject: A decision-process question
says: asks how the buyer's organisation reaches a yes and who signs it off
brings approvals to light that would otherwise appear at the last minute
cards.use: need to learn who else must agree before a purchase can happen
not: asks which package the buyer prefers

cards.subject: A next-step agreement
says: ends the call with a dated action for both sides
prevents a call from ending in a vague promise to be in touch
cards.use: are about to end a call that went well but has no follow-up booked
not: is left to the buyer to propose after the call

cards.subject: Pitching before diagnosing
says: presents a solution before the buyer's problem is understood
pushes the buyer into comparing features and then price
cards.use: notice a seller describing features in the first minutes of a call
not: builds trust faster than asking questions

cards.subject: A qualified lead
says: has a real need, the means to pay and a reason to act within a realistic time
deserves a seller's time more than a casual enquiry does
cards.use: must decide whether an enquiry is worth a proposal
not: is any person who has filled in a contact form

cards.subject: A sales opportunity
says: is a qualified lead with a defined need and a possible deal value in the pipeline
is tracked through stages until it is won or lost
cards.use: need to record a qualified prospect and its likely value
not: is an unvetted name on a purchased list

cards.subject: BANT
says: checks budget, authority, need and timeline
is a four-part checklist for deciding whether a lead is worth pursuing
cards.use: want a quick checklist for a first qualification call
not: scores a lead only on how much it has engaged with emails

cards.subject: Budget
says: asks whether the buyer has money set aside or can get it approved
is the BANT letter that deals with the ability to pay
cards.use: wonder whether the prospect can afford what you are discussing
not: asks who makes the final decision

cards.subject: Authority
says: asks whether the person on the call can decide or strongly influence the purchase
is the BANT letter that deals with who decides
cards.use: suspect the contact is passing messages to someone more senior
not: asks when the result must be delivered

cards.subject: An economic buyer
says: holds the budget and can say yes without asking anyone else
may never attend the early calls yet decides the outcome
cards.use: have a friendly contact who cannot sign anything
not: is always the person who uses the service day to day

cards.subject: A champion
says: is an internal advocate who sells on the seller's behalf when the seller is absent
needs ammunition such as a short summary and proof to make the case internally
cards.use: have a contact inside the buyer who wants the project to succeed
not: is the person who signs the contract

cards.subject: Disqualifying a lead
says: ends the pursuit of a prospect who cannot or will not buy
frees time for prospects with a better chance
cards.use: realise the prospect has no budget, no urgency and no authority
not: shows that the seller has failed at selling

cards.subject: A stage exit checklist
says: defines the evidence required before a deal moves to the next pipeline stage
stops a hopeful deal from inflating the forecast
cards.use: see deals sitting in a late stage with no agreed next step
not: lets each seller move a deal whenever they feel optimistic

cards.subject: A no-decision outcome
says: is a lost deal where the buyer chooses to do nothing
is often a bigger loss than losing to a competitor
cards.use: review why qualified deals keep stalling with no competitor named
not: always means the price was too high

cards.subject: A fixed-price quote
says: commits to one price for a defined scope
moves the risk of overruns to the supplier
cards.use: need a price the buyer can budget exactly for a clearly bounded job
not: bills for every hour worked whatever the scope

cards.subject: Time and materials
says: bills for the time actually worked at an agreed rate
moves the risk of scope growth to the buyer
cards.use: must start work whose scope cannot yet be defined
not: guarantees the final cost to the buyer

cards.subject: A day rate
says: prices one person's working day at an agreed figure
is the unit used to estimate and bill time-based work
cards.use: need to price consultancy or build work by the day
not: covers a monthly allocation of unspecified work

cards.subject: A retainer
says: bills a regular amount for ongoing availability or an allocation of work
gives the supplier predictable income and the client priority access
cards.use: serve a client who needs continuing help rather than a single project
not: is paid only once a project is delivered

cards.subject: Tiered pricing
says: offers several packages at rising prices with more included at each step
lets the buyer pick the level that suits them
cards.use: sell to clients whose needs range from basic to demanding
not: charges the same price to every buyer for the same work

cards.subject: A scope statement
says: lists what is included and what is excluded from the price
is the document that settles later arguments about whether something was covered
cards.use: need to avoid a client assuming extra work is part of the price
not: states only the total price

cards.subject: An assumptions list
says: records the conditions the price depends on, such as content arriving on time
gives the supplier grounds to reprice if a condition proves false
cards.use: know the estimate relies on the client supplying material
not: lists the features the supplier hopes to add later

cards.subject: A change request
says: prices extra work outside the agreed scope before it begins
keeps scope growth visible and agreed in writing
cards.use: hear a client ask for something that was not in the quote
not: is absorbed quietly to keep the client happy

cards.subject: Value-based pricing
says: sets the price from the worth of the outcome to the buyer
needs the discovery work to establish what the problem costs
cards.use: know a small piece of work removes a very large cost for the client
not: multiplies hours by a standard rate

cards.subject: A payment terms clause
says: states when invoices fall due and any deposit or milestone payments
sets out the cash-flow expectations for both sides
cards.use: need to say when the client pays and in what stages
not: lists what the client will receive

cards.subject: A conditional discount
says: is offered in exchange for something such as a longer commitment or a faster decision
protects the supplier's price by tying any reduction to a return
cards.use: are asked for a discount by a buyer who is ready to proceed
not: is given freely whenever a buyer asks

cards.subject: An executive summary
says: gives the decision-maker the problem, solution, price and next step in a page or less
is the part of a proposal most likely to be read in full
cards.use: write for a senior reader who will not read the whole document
not: lists every task in the project plan

cards.subject: A problem statement
says: restates the buyer's problem in their own terms
proves to the buyer that the seller listened in discovery
cards.use: begin a proposal and want the buyer to recognise their own situation
not: describes the supplier's history and awards

cards.subject: A proposed solution
says: explains how the work will resolve the buyer's problem
ties each part of the offer to a need the buyer raised
cards.use: need to show that the work follows from the buyer's own priorities
not: lists generic services the supplier offers every client

cards.subject: A deliverables list
says: names the concrete things the buyer will receive
lets the buyer check later whether the work was delivered
cards.use: need to say exactly what is handed over at the end
not: describes the supplier's working method in general

cards.subject: A timeline with milestones
says: sets out the order of the work and the dates by which key points are reached
shows where the buyer's own input is needed
cards.use: need to show when the work will happen and what each side must supply
not: states only the final delivery date

cards.subject: A pricing section
says: shows the cost options and what each includes
sits beside the scope so that price and content are read together
cards.use: present the cost of the work in the proposal
not: is placed before the problem is described

cards.subject: A case study
says: backs up claims with a real, evidenced example of earlier work
reduces the buyer's perceived risk
cards.use: meet a buyer who doubts the supplier can deliver
not: can include invented results if they sound plausible

cards.subject: A risks and assumptions section
says: lists what could go wrong and what the plan takes for granted
sets expectations before the work starts rather than after a problem appears
cards.use: know the plan depends on factors outside the supplier's control
not: is left out so the proposal appears more confident

cards.subject: An acceptance criterion
says: states the condition under which a deliverable counts as complete
turns a subjective view of quality into something checkable
cards.use: want to avoid a dispute over whether a deliverable is finished
not: describes the supplier's preferred working hours

cards.subject: A mutual action plan
says: lists the steps both buyer and seller will take to reach a decision and start
gives dates to the buyer's internal approvals as well as the seller's tasks
cards.use: need to keep a long deal moving through the buyer's internal steps
not: lists only the supplier's tasks

cards.subject: Signed acceptance
says: turns a proposal into an agreement
records that the buyer agrees to the scope, price and terms
cards.use: need written confirmation before any work begins
not: is implied whenever the client replies politely

cards.subject: An objection
says: is a concern a buyer raises that stands between them and a decision
is often a sign of real engagement rather than rejection
cards.use: need the general term for any concern a prospect raises before deciding
not: means the buyer has decided not to buy

cards.subject: Arguing with the buyer
says: wins the point and loses the relationship
puts the buyer on the defensive
cards.use: feel the urge to prove that the buyer is wrong
not: is a reliable way to resolve an objection

cards.subject: Acknowledge and clarify
says: repeats the concern and asks what is behind it before answering
stops the seller from answering the wrong question
cards.use: hear an objection and are about to launch an answer
not: answers immediately with a prepared script

cards.subject: A price objection
says: is answered by returning to the cost of the problem and the value of the fix
is not met by cutting the figure at once
cards.use: hear that the quote is too expensive
not: is solved by an immediate discount

cards.subject: A timing objection
says: is explored by asking what would need to change and what waiting costs
often hides an unaddressed budget or priority problem
cards.use: hear that now is not a good time
not: is a final refusal to be accepted

cards.subject: Isolating the objection
says: asks whether this concern is the only thing standing in the way
prevents a new objection appearing as soon as one is resolved
cards.use: have answered a concern and want to know whether a deal is now possible
not: ignores the buyer's other concerns

cards.subject: A stall such as we will think about it
says: is explored by asking what specifically needs thinking about
ends with a follow-up date agreed on the call
cards.use: hear a polite non-answer at the end of a proposal call
not: is accepted as a final answer and logged as lost

cards.subject: A competitor comparison
says: is handled by asking what the buyer values and showing fit
avoids criticising the competitor
cards.use: learn that the buyer is also talking to another supplier
not: is answered by criticising the rival's weaknesses

cards.subject: A trust objection
says: is answered with evidence such as references, real results and a clear process
cannot be argued away with assurances alone
cards.use: meet a buyer who doubts the supplier will deliver
not: is dismissed as the buyer being difficult

cards.subject: An authority objection
says: is handled by offering to join the conversation or to equip the buyer with a summary for the decision-maker
turns I need to check with my boss into a planned next step
cards.use: hear that someone else has to approve the purchase
not: is a reason to stop talking to the contact

cards.subject: A kickoff meeting
says: brings client and delivery team together at the start to agree goals, roles and the plan
sets the tone for the working relationship
cards.use: have just won a project and need to start well
not: is held after the first deliverable

cards.subject: A welcome pack
says: tells the new client who to contact, how to ask for help and what happens next
reduces the client's uncertainty in the first days
cards.use: want a new client to know how everything works from day one
not: is the contract the client signs

cards.subject: An onboarding checklist
says: lists every step from signature to a working service so none is forgotten
is used the same way for every client
cards.use: need to make the start of every engagement consistent
not: is rewritten from memory for each client

cards.subject: Access and asset collection
says: gathers logins, content, brand files and approvals the delivery team needs
is a common source of delay when left until late
cards.use: know the project cannot progress without material from the client
not: is requested only after the build is finished

cards.subject: A single point of contact
says: gives the client one named person to ask for anything
prevents requests being lost between team members
cards.use: see a client emailing three different colleagues about the same issue
not: is replaced by a shared inbox nobody owns

cards.subject: Setting expectations
says: agrees what the client can expect and by when, before anything goes wrong
prevents disappointment by naming limits and timescales early
cards.use: know the client assumes a quicker turnaround than the supplier can offer
not: promises the fastest outcome to win goodwill

cards.subject: A sales-to-delivery handover note
says: records what was discussed, promised and agreed in the sales process
prevents the delivery team from having to rediscover the client's priorities
cards.use: pass a newly won client from the seller to the delivery team
not: contains only the signed price

cards.subject: A success criterion
says: states how the client will judge whether the engagement worked
is agreed during onboarding and revisited at reviews
cards.use: want to know in advance how the client will measure the result
not: is decided by the supplier alone after delivery

cards.subject: A go-live checklist
says: confirms every item that must be true before the service or site is switched on
includes testing, backups and a rollback route
cards.use: are about to launch the client's work to the public
not: is written after launch

cards.subject: An early churn signal
says: shows up as missed meetings, slow replies or unused features in the first weeks
gives the team time to rescue a relationship before cancellation
cards.use: see a new client going quiet shortly after signing
not: only appears at renewal time

cards.subject: A support ticket
says: records one client request or problem with an owner and a status
is the single record that follows an issue to resolution
cards.use: receive a problem report that must not be lost
not: is a private note kept in one person's inbox

cards.subject: Triage
says: sorts incoming requests by urgency, impact and owner
decides what is handled first and by whom
cards.use: face a queue of new requests of mixed importance
not: resolves every request in the order it arrived

cards.subject: Severity
says: describes how badly the issue affects the client's service
is set by impact, not by how loudly the client asks
cards.use: need to rate how serious a fault is
not: sets the order in which the team works through the queue

cards.subject: Priority
says: sets the order in which the team will work, taking impact and urgency into account
can differ from severity when a lesser fault has a hard deadline
cards.use: have to decide which of several open issues to do first
not: is the technical measure of damage alone

cards.subject: A runbook
says: gives step-by-step instructions for a known task or fault
lets any trained team member perform the task the same way
cards.use: meet a recurring problem that has a known fix
not: records only the cause after the event

cards.subject: A knowledge base article
says: explains a question or fix in a form clients can find and follow themselves
lowers the number of tickets for common questions
cards.use: see the same how-do-I question arriving every week
not: is an internal record of staff disciplinary actions

cards.subject: A workaround
says: restores the client's ability to work without fixing the underlying cause
buys time while a lasting fix is arranged
cards.use: cannot yet fix the root of the fault but the client is blocked
not: is the permanent solution

cards.subject: A set of reproduction steps
says: describes the exact actions that make a fault appear
lets a second person see the same fault
cards.use: need to pass a defect to a developer who cannot see the client's screen
not: states only that something is broken

cards.subject: An incident
says: is an unplanned interruption to a service or a drop in its quality
is handled first to restore service, not to find blame
cards.use: see a client's site go down unexpectedly
not: is the hidden cause behind a series of faults

cards.subject: A problem record
says: tracks the underlying cause of one or more incidents
exists so that the cause is fixed rather than the symptom repeatedly patched
cards.use: see the same incident recurring every few weeks
not: is closed as soon as service is restored

cards.subject: Root cause analysis
says: seeks the underlying reason a fault happened rather than the visible trigger
asks why repeatedly until a fixable cause is reached
cards.use: want to stop a failure returning after it has been fixed once
not: names the person responsible for the error

cards.subject: A blameless post-incident review
says: studies what happened and how the system allowed it, without assigning blame to a person
produces actions to prevent or detect the same failure
cards.use: have just resolved a serious incident and want the team to learn from it
not: identifies who should be disciplined

cards.subject: A service level agreement
says: is a written commitment to defined service levels between supplier and client
states what the client can expect and what happens if it is missed
cards.use: need to agree in writing how quickly a supplier will respond and resolve
not: is a marketing slogan

cards.subject: First response time
says: measures how long a client waits for a meaningful first reply
counts a real reply, not an automatic acknowledgement
cards.use: want to measure how quickly the client hears from a person
not: measures how long the fix takes

cards.subject: Resolution time
says: measures how long the issue takes to be resolved
is usually longer than the first response time
cards.use: want to measure how long the client's problem stays open
not: measures how quickly the first reply arrives

cards.subject: Business hours cover
says: counts only the agreed working hours toward a response target
means a request sent out of hours waits until the next working period starts
cards.use: see a ticket raised on a Friday evening for a service with working-hours support
not: covers every hour of every day

cards.subject: Uptime
says: measures the share of time a service is available
is expressed as a percentage over a stated period
cards.use: need a figure for how reliably a service is running
not: measures how fast pages load

cards.subject: A service level indicator
says: is the measured quantity such as latency or the proportion of successful requests
provides the data a target is judged against
cards.use: need to decide what exactly to measure for a service
not: is the target the team sets itself

cards.subject: A service level objective
says: is the internal target set for an indicator
is usually set tighter than any promise made to the client
cards.use: want an internal target that leaves room before the contractual commitment is at risk
not: is the contractual promise to the client

cards.subject: A service credit
says: compensates the client with a reduction when agreed levels are missed
is the usual remedy written into the agreement
cards.use: need to define what the client receives when the supplier misses a target
not: is a gift offered at renewal

cards.subject: An SLA exclusion
says: lists the events that do not count against the target, such as planned maintenance or client-caused faults
must be written clearly to avoid disputes
cards.use: need to say that a client's own change that breaks the site is not a breach
not: lets the supplier ignore any missed target it chooses

cards.subject: Pausing the clock
says: stops the response timer while the team is waiting on the client
reflects that the supplier cannot progress without information
cards.use: wait for a client to provide logins before a fix can start
not: hides slow work from the client

cards.subject: A percentile response target
says: states the time within which a stated share of tickets, such as nine in ten, will be answered
is more honest than an average that hides slow outliers
cards.use: see an average response time that looks good while some clients wait for days
not: promises every single ticket will meet the target

cards.subject: Functional escalation
says: passes a ticket to a specialist with deeper technical skill
is used when the first-line agent has reached the limit of their knowledge
cards.use: meet a fault that needs a developer or a systems engineer
not: brings in a manager to authorise a refund

cards.subject: Hierarchical escalation
says: brings in a more senior person for authority, resources or a decision
is used when the client's concern needs a decision beyond the agent's remit
cards.use: need approval beyond your own authority
not: transfers the ticket to a technical specialist

cards.subject: An escalation rule
says: defines in advance when a ticket must be passed on
stops escalation depending on one person's judgement or nerve
cards.use: see agents sitting on difficult tickets rather than asking for help
not: is decided only after a client complains

cards.subject: An escalation trigger
says: is a specific condition such as an at-risk response target or a repeated contact that starts the escalation
makes escalation automatic rather than discretionary
cards.use: want a ticket to move up when its response target is about to be missed
not: is a client's request to speak to someone senior

cards.subject: A warm handoff
says: introduces the client to the next person and passes the full context
spares the client from explaining the problem again
cards.use: pass a distressed client to a specialist
not: transfers the ticket without a word to either party

cards.subject: A single accountable owner
says: keeps one named person responsible for the client even when many contribute
prevents everyone assuming someone else is handling it
cards.use: see a serious issue with five people involved and no one updating the client
not: is replaced by a committee decision

cards.subject: A major incident
says: is a serious service failure that justifies a coordinated response outside the normal ticket flow
has a named coordinator and regular updates to the clients affected
cards.use: see several clients' services fail together
not: is any ticket marked urgent by a client

cards.subject: An incident commander
says: coordinates the response, assigns tasks and keeps the clients informed
does not usually do the hands-on fixing
cards.use: need one person to run the response to a major failure
not: is the engineer who finds the root cause

cards.subject: An update cadence
says: promises the client a fresh update at regular intervals until the issue is closed
is kept even when the update says nothing has changed
cards.use: have a long-running issue where the client keeps asking for news
not: updates the client only when the fix is ready

cards.subject: A renewal
says: continues a service for another term
is easiest when the client has seen clear value throughout the term
cards.use: approach the end of a client's agreed term
not: is an automatic event requiring no effort from the supplier

cards.subject: Churn
says: is the loss of a client who stops buying
is measured as the share of clients or revenue lost over a period
cards.use: want to measure how many clients are leaving
not: is the growth in new clients

cards.subject: An upsell
says: sells a higher tier or more of the same service to an existing client
is justified by a need the client has already shown
cards.use: see a client outgrowing the package they bought
not: sells a different product to a new client

cards.subject: A cross-sell
says: sells a different product or service to an existing client
builds on the trust already earned in the first relationship
cards.use: know a client has a need that a second service could meet
not: sells a bigger version of the same package

cards.subject: A scheduled account review
says: meets the client at regular intervals to review results and plan ahead
gives a natural place to raise renewal and new needs
cards.use: want a routine to keep a client relationship healthy
not: takes place only when the client is threatening to leave

cards.subject: A value recap
says: reminds the client of the results delivered during the term
is prepared before the renewal conversation starts
cards.use: need evidence that the service has been worth the cost
not: lists the supplier's costs

cards.subject: An early renewal conversation
says: starts well before the term ends so there is time to fix any concerns
avoids discussing renewal for the first time when the client is already deciding
cards.use: have an account whose term ends in three months
not: waits until the notice period has passed

cards.subject: An expansion trigger
says: is an event such as growth in traffic or new staff that signals a need for more
makes the upsell conversation timely and relevant
cards.use: notice a client's usage nearing the limits of its package
not: is a calendar date for a sales campaign

cards.subject: Auto-renewal
says: continues the agreement unless the client gives notice within a set period
calls for a clear reminder to the client before the notice date
cards.use: have an agreement that rolls on from term to term
not: ends the agreement when the term finishes

cards.subject: Net revenue retention
says: compares revenue from the same group of clients at the start and end of a period, including upgrades and losses
can exceed 100 percent when expansion outweighs churn
cards.use: want one figure that combines churn with upsell
not: counts only newly won clients

cards.subject: Prompt acknowledgement
says: tells the client straight away that their message has been received and who has it
reduces anxiety even before an answer is ready
cards.use: receive a message you cannot answer fully today
not: waits until the full answer is ready

cards.subject: Plain language
says: replaces jargon with words the client uses themselves
makes sure the reader can act on the message
cards.use: write to a client who is not technical
not: shows the supplier's expertise by using technical terms

cards.subject: A meeting summary
says: records the decisions, actions and owners straight after a call
is the written record that settles later disagreements about what was agreed
cards.use: have just finished a call where several things were agreed
not: is sent only if a dispute arises later

cards.subject: Telling bad news early
says: gives the client time to react and plan
is accompanied by what is being done and a revised date
cards.use: know a deadline will be missed
not: waits until the deadline passes in the hope of catching up
like: An apology that names the fix

cards.subject: An apology that names the fix
says: acknowledges the specific mistake, states its effect and says what is being done
does not shift blame onto the client
cards.use: have made an error that affected a client's business
not: says sorry for any inconvenience without naming what went wrong

cards.subject: Saying no with an alternative
says: declines a request while offering something the supplier can do
keeps the conversation going where a bare refusal ends it
cards.use: are asked for something outside scope or capability
not: agrees to everything to avoid conflict

cards.subject: A single email thread per issue
says: keeps the history of one matter in one place
keeps the history of one matter in a single email conversation
cards.use: see one issue spread across many unrelated email chains
not: starts a new thread for every reply

cards.subject: Choosing call over email
says: is the better channel when a matter is emotional, complex or going back and forth
is followed by a written summary
cards.use: have exchanged six emails and the misunderstanding is growing
not: is chosen because it avoids a written record

cards.subject: Recording decisions
says: notes what was decided, by whom and on what date
stops a verbal agreement being remembered differently by each party
cards.use: hear a client approve a change by phone
not: trusts memory for important agreements

cards.subject: A status report
says: tells the client what was done, what is next and what needs their input
is sent on a regular rhythm that the client knows in advance
cards.use: run a project that lasts weeks and want the client informed without asking
not: is sent only when problems arise

cards.subject: Not over-promising
says: commits only to what can be delivered and says so openly
builds a reputation for doing what is said
cards.use: feel pressure to promise a date you are unsure of
not: agrees to the client's date to keep them happy

cards.subject: The Qualified deal stage
says: is the first stage in the GGLink CRM pipeline
carries a default win probability of 25 percent
cards.use: need the GGLink pipeline stage with a default probability of 25 percent
not: carries a default probability of 50 percent

cards.subject: The Proposal sent deal stage
says: follows Qualified in the GGLink CRM pipeline
carries a default win probability of 50 percent
cards.use: need the GGLink stage for a deal once a proposal has gone out
not: carries a default probability of 75 percent

cards.subject: The Negotiation deal stage
says: comes after Proposal sent in the GGLink CRM pipeline
carries a default win probability of 75 percent
cards.use: need the GGLink stage for a deal where terms are being agreed
not: carries a default probability of 25 percent

cards.subject: The Won deal stage
says: closes a GGLink deal as a success
carries a default win probability of 100 percent
cards.use: need the GGLink stage whose default probability is 100 percent
not: carries a default probability of 75 percent

cards.subject: The Lost deal stage
says: closes a GGLink deal as a failure
carries a default win probability of 0 percent
cards.use: need the GGLink stage whose default probability is 0 percent
not: carries a default probability of 25 percent

cards.subject: The weighted pipeline
says: is the sum of each deal's value multiplied by its probability, divided by 100
gives a more realistic forecast than the raw total of open deal values
cards.use: want a forecast figure that reflects how likely each GGLink deal is to close
not: adds up the full value of every open deal

cards.subject: Contact consent
says: is stored on every GGLink contact as consent, consent_date and consent_source
is a first-class field, not an afterthought
cards.use: need to know where a GGLink contact's permission to be emailed is recorded
not: is recorded only in the nurture campaign settings

cards.subject: A mailable contact
says: has consent of consented, soft or legitimate, a status that is not unsubscribed or bounced, and an email address
is the only kind of GGLink contact included in a bulk email
cards.use: decide whether a contact may be included in a GGLink bulk email
not: is any contact with an email address

cards.subject: A contact with unknown or withdrawn consent
says: is not mailable in a GGLink bulk email
is excluded whatever the contact's deal history
cards.use: find a contact whose consent is unknown or opted out
not: may be emailed if they have an open deal

cards.subject: A nurture sequence send log
says: records what a GGLink nurture sequence has sent to each contact
ensures nobody is emailed the same step twice
cards.use: worry that a contact could receive the same nurture email twice
not: replaces the need for consent records

cards.subject: A product interest tag
says: is stored in the GGLink CRM inside a comma-wrapped string such as ,crm,ecommerce,
allows exact matching so one tag cannot half-match another
cards.use: need to filter GGLink contacts by a product interest without false matches
not: is a free-text note that cannot be filtered

cards.subject: The GGLink enquiry flow
says: sends a website contact form to the Enquiries section of the admin and sends a notification email
is protected from spam by reCAPTCHA
cards.use: need to follow what happens when a visitor submits the GGLink contact form
not: posts the enquiry to a public page

cards.subject: Enquiry email deliverability
says: depends on verifying the whole GGLink domain in SendGrid so SPF and DKIM are set up
fails if the sender in SENDGRID_FROM is not a verified sender
cards.use: find that GGLink enquiry notifications go to spam or are rejected
not: is fixed by turning off the reCAPTCHA

cards.subject: The GGLink CRM size design
says: was built for about 100,000 contacts
indexes every filtered or sorted column and paginates lists on the server
cards.use: ask how the GGLink CRM copes with very large contact lists
not: loads the whole contact table into the browser

cards.subject: The GGLink admin roles
says: are owner and editor
never allow the last owner to be removed or demoted
cards.use: need to know which roles GGLink's admin has
not: are admin, manager and viewer

cards.subject: One source of truth per customer object
says: names a single tool as the owner of each object such as the customer record
avoids two tools both believing they own the record
cards.use: are choosing CRM, scheduling, helpdesk and chat tools for an agency's sales and support
not: lets each tool keep its own copy of the customer to save time

cards.subject: The GG_PRICING_LIVE switch
says: keeps GGLink prices hidden until they are real
is one of two master switches in gg-sales-config.php
cards.use: need to know how GGLink stops unreal prices appearing publicly
not: controls client results rather than prices

cards.subject: The GG_RESULTS_LIVE switch
says: keeps GGLink client results hidden until they are real
is one of two master switches in gg-sales-config.php
cards.use: need to know how GGLink stops unreal outcomes appearing publicly
not: controls published prices rather than results

cards.subject: A published price
says: is a claim the business can be held to
falls under the CAP Code for advertising
cards.use: ask why GGLink does not show prices before they are real
not: is only an estimate that need not be honoured

cards.subject: A published result
says: must be a real, anonymised number the business could evidence
falls under the DMCC Act 2024 where it is a testimonial or customer result
cards.use: ask what GGLink needs before showing a client result
not: can be rounded up to look more impressive

cards.subject: Evidence for a result
says: is what GGLink must be able to produce if a customer or the ASA asks
means any result that cannot be backed up should be deleted
cards.use: find a result on the site that nobody can back up
not: is optional when the result is anonymised

cards.subject: A published service level
says: such as a response time, uptime or backup retention is published only if it can be evidenced and met
is not committed to in advance of real capacity
cards.use: feel tempted to quote a response time to a prospect that has never been checked
not: can be copied from a competitor to look competitive

cards.subject: The Pricing section of the GGLink admin
says: holds care plans and day rates
stays hidden on the public site until it has real values
cards.use: need to know where GGLink's care plans and day rates are entered
not: publishes placeholder values automatically
like: The Credentials section of the GGLink admin

cards.subject: The Credentials section of the GGLink admin
says: holds certificate numbers
stays hidden on the public site until it has real values
cards.use: need to know where GGLink's certificate numbers are entered
not: holds day rates and care plans
like: The Pricing section of the GGLink admin

cards.subject: A placeholder in the repository sales config
says: for a GGLink price or service level is a TODO marker rather than a real figure
means no price or support commitment should be quoted from the repository copy
cards.use: see a TODO in the sales config where a price should be
not: is a real price waiting to go live

qa.q: In a discovery call, which opening question is most likely to draw out the buyer's real situation?
qa.right: Can you tell me what led you to get in touch?
wrong: Do you have a budget for this?
Would you like to see our prices?
Are you ready to start next month?
qa.why: An open question invites a full answer; the others are closed and jump ahead.

qa.q: What is the main purpose of qualifying a lead?
qa.right: To decide whether the prospect has the need, means and reason to buy so effort goes to the right deals
wrong: To make the prospect feel special before the quote
To collect contact details for the mailing list
To prove to the prospect that the seller's product is best
qa.why: Qualification protects the seller's time and the accuracy of the forecast.

qa.q: A client asks for a price on a clearly defined job that will not change. Which quote type suits it?
qa.right: A fixed-price quote
wrong: An open-ended time-and-materials estimate
A retainer billed monthly
A day rate with no scope
qa.why: A well-bounded scope is what fixed pricing needs.

qa.q: Which of these best describes tiered pricing?
qa.right: Several packages at rising prices, with more included at each step
wrong: One price that is negotiated separately for each client
A discount that rises the longer a client waits
A price quoted in a different currency for each region
qa.why: Tiers let buyers choose the level that fits them.

qa.q: Why should a support ticket have a single named owner?
qa.right: So that the client and the team know who is responsible for the next step
wrong: So the other team members can ignore the ticket
So the client is charged per person involved
So the ticket can be closed without a reply
qa.why: An unowned ticket is the one that gets dropped.

qa.q: What is the first thing a good support agent does when a message cannot be answered fully today?
qa.right: Acknowledge receipt and say who is working on it
wrong: Wait until the full answer is ready
Forward it to a manager
Ask the client to resend it tomorrow
qa.why: A prompt acknowledgement reduces anxiety even before an answer exists.

qa.q: What does a renewal conversation depend on most?
qa.right: The client having seen clear value during the term
wrong: The supplier sending the invoice early
The client having no alternatives
The supplier offering a large discount first
qa.why: Value delivered and recorded is what makes renewal easy.

qa.q: A prospect says, 'The price is too high.' What should the seller do first?
qa.right: Acknowledge the concern and ask what they are comparing it with
wrong: Offer 10 percent off immediately
Explain that competitors charge more
End the call and send a shorter quote
qa.why: Clarifying shows what the objection really is; an instant discount teaches the buyer to haggle.

qa.q: A ticket describes a total outage of a client's site, but the client is relaxed in tone. How should it be rated?
qa.right: High severity, because severity follows impact rather than tone
wrong: Low severity, because the client is not worried
Medium, because it is the client's first ticket
Unrated until the client raises their voice
qa.why: Severity measures effect on the service, not the client's manner.

qa.q: Which pair of measures does a service level agreement usually set?
qa.right: First response time and resolution time
wrong: Number of staff and office opening hours
Page count and word count
Price and discount level
qa.why: These are the standard commitments in a support agreement.

qa.q: A sales call ends with 'Great, I will be in touch.' What is missing?
qa.right: A dated next step agreed by both sides
wrong: A final price discount
A signed contract
A summary of competitors
qa.why: A vague ending lets deals drift.

qa.q: A proposal starts with a page about the supplier's history. The buyer is a busy director. What change helps most?
qa.right: Open with an executive summary of the buyer's problem, the solution, the price and the next step
wrong: Move the history to the end and delete the price
Add more case studies at the front
Make the font smaller to fit more content
qa.why: A senior reader decides from the first page.

qa.q: Which statement about upselling is correct?
qa.right: It is strongest when it responds to a need the client has already shown
wrong: It works best at the first meeting before any need is shown
It means selling a different product to a new client
It should be avoided because it harms trust
qa.why: Relevant upsells grow from usage and outcomes.

qa.q: A new client has paid the deposit but has not provided logins or content, and the project has stalled. Which onboarding step would have prevented this?
qa.right: Collecting access and assets at kickoff, with dates
wrong: Offering a discount for early payment
Sending a longer welcome email
Raising the price to cover delays
qa.why: Client dependencies need dates agreed at the start.

qa.q: What is a mailable contact in the GGLink CRM?
qa.right: A contact with consent of consented, soft or legitimate, a status that is not unsubscribed or bounced, and an email address
wrong: Any contact who has opened an email in the last year
Any contact who has an open deal
Any contact imported from a spreadsheet
qa.why: Consent and status together decide mailability.

qa.q: In the GGLink CRM, which stage carries a default probability of 50 percent?
qa.right: Proposal sent
wrong: Qualified
Negotiation
Lost
qa.why: Qualified is 25, Proposal sent 50, Negotiation 75, Won 100 and Lost 0.

qa.q: Three GGLink deals are open: 10,000 at Qualified, 20,000 at Proposal sent and 8,000 at Negotiation. What is the weighted pipeline?
qa.why: Weighted pipeline is value times probability divided by 100: 2,500 + 10,000 + 6,000 = 18,500.

qa.q: A support agreement promises a first response within 4 business hours, with business hours 09:00 to 17:00 Monday to Friday. A ticket arrives on Friday at 16:00. By when must the first response be sent?
qa.right: Monday at 12:00
wrong: Friday at 20:00
Saturday at 16:00
Monday at 09:00
qa.why: One hour is used on Friday and three remain from Monday 09:00, ending Monday 12:00.

qa.q: A client asks for a feature during build that is not in the scope statement. What should the account manager do?
qa.right: Price it as a change request and agree it in writing before starting
wrong: Add it quietly to keep the client happy
Refuse to discuss anything outside the quote
Include it and raise the price of the next project
qa.why: A change request keeps the scope visible and agreed.

qa.q: A buyer says, 'We will think about it.' Which reply is best?
qa.right: Ask what in particular they need to think about and agree a date to speak again
wrong: Say thanks and wait for them to call
Offer an immediate discount to prompt a decision
Send three further case studies the same day
qa.why: The real objection is hidden until it is asked about.

qa.q: A friendly contact keeps telling you the project is a great idea but cannot sign off anything. What should you do?
qa.right: Identify the economic buyer and ask the contact to help arrange access
wrong: Send the contract to the contact and wait
Treat the deal as won because the contact is positive
Stop contacting them and look for a new lead
qa.why: A champion needs to be connected to a person who holds budget and decides.

qa.q: Your team keeps solving the same recurring fault with a workaround. What should be opened?
qa.right: A problem record to find and fix the underlying cause
wrong: A new incident each time with no link to the others
A service credit for the client
A note saying the fault is normal
qa.why: Incidents are restored; problems are fixed at the cause.

qa.q: A client sends an angry message about repeated downtime. What should the first reply do?
qa.right: Acknowledge the impact, say who owns it and when the next update will come
wrong: Defend the team with the uptime figures
Wait until a fix is ready before replying
Copy in the client's senior colleagues to show seriousness
qa.why: Acknowledge and commit to an update before anything else.

qa.q: You must decide between a warm handoff and a cold transfer for a client who has already explained the fault twice. Which should you choose, and why?
qa.right: A warm handoff, because the next person receives the full context and the client does not repeat themselves
wrong: A cold transfer, because it is faster for the first agent
A cold transfer, because it protects the specialist from interruption
Neither: tell the client to open a new ticket
qa.why: Context should travel with the client.

qa.q: A prospect asks a GGLink seller for the support response time. The repository config still holds TODO placeholders for service levels. What is the right answer?
qa.right: Do not quote a figure; service levels are published only if they can be evidenced and met
wrong: Quote a typical industry response time
Quote the fastest time you think is achievable
Quote four business hours as a standard
qa.why: Unevidenced service-level claims are not to be made.

qa.q: A GGLink seller wants to add a customer outcome to the website, 'We doubled their enquiries', but cannot find the numbers. What should happen?
qa.right: It should not be published until it is a real, anonymised result that can be evidenced
wrong: Publish it with a small disclaimer
Round the number to the nearest convenient figure
Publish it if the client agrees verbally
qa.why: Published results are claims; the GG_RESULTS_LIVE switch exists to hold them back until they are real.

qa.q: Which contact would the GGLink CRM include in a bulk email?
qa.right: A contact with soft consent, status active and an email address
wrong: A contact with unknown consent and an open deal
A contact who has unsubscribed but is a past client
A contact with consent but an empty email field
qa.why: Consent, status and email all have to qualify.

qa.q: A renewal is due in ninety days and the account's usage has dropped. What should the account manager do first?
qa.right: Contact the client to understand the drop and offer help before discussing renewal terms
wrong: Wait until the last month and then send the renewal invoice
Offer a discount on the renewal immediately
Mark the account as lost
qa.why: Usage falls are an early churn signal; fix the cause first.

qa.q: A support team measures only the average time to first response. It looks fine, but some clients wait days. What would help?
qa.right: Report a percentile target so slow outliers are visible
wrong: Switch to measuring only the fastest reply
Remove the slowest tickets from the data
Raise the target average
qa.why: An average hides outliers; a percentile exposes them.

qa.q: A team is quoting a project with many unknowns. The client wants a fixed price. What is the most sound approach?
qa.right: Run a paid discovery phase first, then fix the price for the defined scope
wrong: Quote a fixed price with a large hidden margin
Quote a low fixed price and recover the cost through changes
Decline because fixed prices are never appropriate
qa.why: Reducing uncertainty before fixing a price shares risk fairly.

qa.q: Your deals often sit in Negotiation for months and then vanish with no competitor named. What should you examine first?
qa.right: Whether the stage exit criteria, stakeholder map and decision process were established before reaching Negotiation
wrong: Whether the quote font was too small
Whether the discount authority needs raising
Whether more leads could be added to the top of the pipeline
qa.why: These deals are no-decision outcomes caused by weak qualification.

qa.q: A client on a three-year agreement asks for a refund after a series of outages. The agreement's service level exclusion covers planned maintenance, and two of the outages were planned. What is the fair way to proceed?
qa.right: Check each outage against the exclusions, apply the service credit only to the unplanned ones and explain the result clearly
wrong: Refund everything to avoid conflict
Refuse any credit because the contract is long
Apply a credit to planned outages as well and hide the reasoning
qa.why: Apply the agreement as written and communicate it openly.

qa.q: A major incident hits several clients at once. Who should coordinate the response and communicate with affected clients?
qa.right: An incident commander, separate from the engineers doing the fix
wrong: The engineer who is finding the cause
Whoever receives the first complaint
The salesperson for each client, independently
qa.why: Separating coordination from fixing keeps both effective.

qa.q: A seller wants to give a 15 percent discount to close a deal. What is the best response from the sales manager?
qa.right: Agree only if the client gives something in return, such as a longer term or a quicker decision
wrong: Agree because winning is more important
Refuse any discount whatever the circumstances
Give 5 percent now and 10 percent later regardless
qa.why: A conditional discount protects value.

qa.q: A prospect objects that the supplier is smaller than a rival. What is the most effective response?
qa.right: Ask what concerns the size raises, then answer with evidence such as references and a clear delivery process
wrong: Point out the rival's recent failures
Offer to match the rival's price
Say size does not matter
qa.why: A trust objection is answered with evidence, not defensiveness or criticism of others.

qa.q: You are choosing tools for an agency's sales and support. Which question should you answer first?
qa.right: Which tool is the single source of truth for each object, such as the customer record
wrong: Which tool has the most integrations
Which tool has the most users
Which tool is cheapest per seat
qa.why: Two tools that both believe they own the customer record are the most common source of trouble.

qa.q: A seller notices a lead has opened every email but never replies, has no budget holder involved and has no date in mind. How should the lead be handled?
qa.right: Keep it in nurture with light contact, and do not forecast it as a live opportunity
wrong: Mark it Proposal sent to encourage progress
Offer a discount to provoke a reply
Delete it from the CRM
qa.why: Engagement alone is not qualification.

qa.q: A client's contract auto-renews unless notice is given 30 days before the end of the term. Which action best protects the relationship?
qa.right: Remind the client well before the notice date and review value with them
wrong: Say nothing so the contract rolls on
Send the reminder after the notice date
Offer a discount only to clients who cancel
qa.why: Auto-renewal should never depend on the client forgetting.

qa.q: A GGLink seller is told a contact's consent is 'unknown'. The contact has an open deal in Negotiation. May they be added to a bulk email?
qa.right: No; unknown consent is not mailable regardless of an open deal
wrong: Yes; an open deal implies consent
Yes; once they have opened a previous email
Yes, but only if the email has an unsubscribe link
qa.why: Mailability depends on consent and status, not deal stage.

qa.q: After a site deploy for a GGLink client, the support agent finds the enquiry form submits but no notification email arrives. The enquiry does appear in the admin. What is the most likely area to check?
qa.right: SendGrid: the verified sender in SENDGRID_FROM and domain verification for SPF and DKIM
wrong: The weighted pipeline settings
The nurture sequence send log
The admin owner and editor roles
qa.why: The enquiry was stored, so the form worked; the problem is mail delivery.

qa.q: A large account has five stakeholders, and the sponsor has just left the company. Renewal is due in two months. What is the strongest plan?
qa.right: Map the remaining stakeholders, find a new sponsor, run a value recap and involve senior people on both sides
wrong: Send the renewal invoice and wait
Offer a large discount to all stakeholders
Assume the account is lost and stop investing
qa.why: A lost champion is a major renewal risk and calls for coordinated action.

qa.q: Two options: a lower price now with a three-year term, or the standard price with a one-year term. The buyer asks you to decide. What question matters most?
qa.right: What each option does to the supplier's margin, cash flow and capacity to serve over the whole term
wrong: Which option is easier to explain
Which option the buyer would like to hear first
Which option makes the first invoice largest
qa.why: Evaluate the full-term effect, not only the headline.

qa.q: A service level objective is set equal to the contractual SLA. What risk does this create?
qa.right: Any miss against the objective is already a breach, leaving no early warning
wrong: The client will receive too many service credits automatically
The team will overperform consistently
The measurements will become less accurate
qa.why: Objectives are usually tighter than promises so there is margin.

qa.q: A seller argues for publishing a client result because it is 'roughly true'. What is the most important point to make?
qa.right: A published result is a claim that must be real and evidenced, or the business risks breaching advertising rules and losing trust
wrong: Rounded results are always acceptable if flattering
Only large numbers need evidence
Evidence is only needed if the client objects
qa.why: Gating results behind a switch protects the business from claims it cannot support.

qa.q: Revenue from existing clients rose 112 percent of last year's figure after upgrades, cancellations and downgrades. What does this say?
qa.right: Net revenue retention is above 100 percent, so expansion outweighed churn
wrong: Churn was zero
New clients drove the whole increase
Upsell revenue was lower than lost revenue
qa.why: NRR counts upgrades and losses from the same group of clients.

qa.q: A support team solves every ticket quickly, yet the number of tickets rises each month. What does this suggest?
qa.right: Recurring causes are not being fixed, so problem management and knowledge articles are needed
wrong: The team should answer even faster
The clients are using the service too much
The severity ratings should be raised
qa.why: Speed in handling symptoms does not reduce demand caused by unfixed causes.

qa.q: Why does a mutual action plan help on a long enterprise deal?
qa.right: It puts dates on the buyer's internal approvals as well as the seller's tasks, exposing delays early
wrong: It forces the buyer to sign sooner
It replaces the proposal
It lets the seller control the buyer's calendar
qa.why: It makes the path to a decision shared and visible.
